data.title: Visolaje – one of the largest Slavic barrow cemeteries
data.excerpt: At the locality of Cesciny-Pravec near Visolaje, on a gentle rise beside the old road through the Váh region, 33 Slavic barrows survive and about 15 more were destroyed by ploughing — which makes the cemetery one of the largest and best preserved in Slovakia. Burial here began at the end of the 8th and the beginning of the 9th century, and the excavation of 1960 recorded cremation graves, a 32 cm iron knife and even a burnt band of earth interpreted as a funeral pyre.
data.metaTitle: Visolaje – one of the largest Slavic barrow cemeteries
data.metaDescription: The Slavic barrow cemetery at Cesciny-Pravec near Visolaje preserves 33 burial mounds and ranks among the largest and best preserved in Slovakia.

children.text:
Visolaje is known above all for the large Slavic barrow cemetery in the locality of Cesciny-Pravec, where 33 barrows of the Slavic period have been recorded. A certain part of them was ploughed over long ago, so the original number of barrows can be determined only approximately. Even so, the barrow cemetery is among the largest in Slovakia. Slavic warriors may have been buried in some of the barrows. The beginnings of burial at this Slavic cemetery can be placed at the end of the 8th and the beginning of the 9th century. 
 
 In early medieval Europe, at the turn of the 7th and 8th centuries, burial under barrows appears in various places, including the territory of present-day Slovakia. The earliest Slavic population brought with it to the territory of present-day Slovakia the custom of cremating the deceased. Around the middle of the 9th century the cremation rite changed into inhumation, in which burial of unburnt bodies began to be preferred. The demise of barrow burial itself was influenced by the beginnings of Christianity, which meant a marked change in the funerary rite. Seven barrow regions are at present known in the territory of Slovakia. The Slavic barrow cemetery at Visolaje, in the locality of Cesciny, is among the best preserved barrow cemeteries in Slovakia today.

This barrow cemetery lies on a gentle rise beside the shortest possible route of the old road through the Váh region. The barrow cemetery at Visolaje is the second largest in northern Slovakia. Thirty-three barrows survive, about 15 more were destroyed by ploughing.

children.text: In the autumn of 1960 the Považie Museum in Žilina carried out an archaeological excavation here, during which it was found that the barrow mounds had been built of earth and small stones obtained from the immediate vicinity. The graves contained charcoal, fragments of pottery from domestic vessels decorated with grooves and multiple wavy lines, fragments of radiolarite cores, stone whetstones of sandstone and so on. In one of the barrows an iron knife 32 cm long was found. Part of the funerary rite was the symbolic addition of a few burnt bones to the grave. In one of the barrows a continuous burnt band of earth enriched with charcoal was found, 5 m long and 1 m wide, which is considered to have been a funeral pyre – a cremation place. This is, however, an isolated find of its kind. The places where the Slavs cremated their dead remain unknown. Only one has so far been confirmed, namely at the barrow cemetery at Kráľovský Chlmec. It is assumed that cremation places lay outside the cemeteries.

In the whole territory of Slovakia the funerary rite was not uniform in this period, just as the manner of building the barrows was not uniform either. The graves in the barrows investigated at Cesciny were cremations, but at the nearby barrow cemetery of Podvrščie at Sverepec, for example, the dead person was not cremated but laid at ground level, lying on his back, and a barrow mound was heaped up over him. At the nearby barrow cemetery at Koscelišče below Malenica the dead were buried in both ways.

children.text: The internal construction of the barrows was likewise different. They were built of materials available in the immediate vicinity. Both cremation and inhumation burials under barrows were lined with stones, or a larger boulder was placed at the feet of the person buried. Once the barrow mound had been heaped up, the boulders were no longer visible on the surface. In some barrows timber rectangular structures were built which served exclusively for the funerary rite – during it they were set alight and, while still burning, covered over.

Wooden posts were set vertically into the barrows. There are several theories about their function (for example, that urns were placed outside the barrow on top of the wooden posts, or beside them; according to another theory, the tops of the posts ended in a figure of one of the pagan deities). The barrows were sometimes separated from the surrounding ground by a trench, which did not encircle the barrow around its whole perimeter but was interrupted in places. Just as the details of the funerary rite differed, so too did the number of burials in a single barrow – from one to as many as eleven persons buried under a single barrow (at the barrow cemetery at Skalica). The ground plans of the individual barrows were not uniform either. Circular and oval barrows occur, and even markedly elongated ones (for example at the barrow cemetery near Horný Lieskov). The only uniform feature is perhaps the position of the barrow cemeteries on lower rises with a view over the surroundings, separated from the settlements by natural obstacles in the form of rivers or valleys. The orientation of the deceased is consistent as well, in an east–west direction, so that their faces were turned towards the rising sun.

children.text: The effort the Slavs devoted to creating their cemeteries was admirable: levelling the ground, digging and carting earth, carrying stone and timber and so on, and all of it at a time when tools were still precious.
